newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices rally on tighter U.S. inventories, Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rally on tighter U.S. inventories, Iraq.

text.p: World oil prices rallied sharply on Wednesday on signs of colder weather on both sides of the Atlantic, a tigher inventory picture and a knee-jerk reaction to what the United States described as "struggles for power" in Iraq.
At the same time, demand for gasoline was expected to grow as inventories were replenished ahead of the spring driving season.
London March futures for international benchmark crude oil Brent blend ended the day's session 52 cents a barrel higher at $22.76.

Private forecaster Weather Services Corp predicted colder temperatures for Europe late in the week and below-normal temperatures for the key heating oil markets in the northeastern United States, which has had some of the coldest weather of the season.

Oil prices were already rallying after the American Petroleum Institute (API) reported on Tuesday night that distillate stocks, including heating oil, fell 2.9 million barrels last week to 119.6 million.
In the northeast United States, the world's largest heating oil market, inventories shed 1.9 million barrels and were 3.6 million lower than a year ago.

"Distillate stocks are drawing down relatively quickly for the moment and particularly for (the northeast U.S.)," said Tony Machacek, an oil broker at Credit Lyonnais Rouse in London. "Gasoline and crude stocks are still generally low compared to previous years."

API said gasoline supplies rose 1.8 million barrels to 201.3 million, but were still a whopping 11.0 million lower than a year ago. Crude stocks, despite a weekly rise of 3.7 million, were 17.7 million below the same time in 1996.
A report from the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration confirmed the inventory changes in the APIs.

"People are starting to focus on the year-on-year gasoline figures," one broker said. "I know it's the middle of winter but in terms of the futures market with the spring contracts, gasoline is starting to be the focus a bit."

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry News added to an already bullish cocktail by saying the United States was closely monitoring the situation in Iraq after reports that President Saddam Hussein had put his wife under house arrest.
But McCurry said there were no indications of troop movements that would suggest any renewed threat to Kuwait.
"It's a good excuse for a market looking to bounce off $22 anyway," said Leslie Nicholas, an energy analyst at GNI Ltd in London.
Under a United Nations oil-for-food exchange, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude oil over six months to pay for humanitarian supplies.
Wednesday's sharp gains came after crude prices lost roughly 10 percent in the last three weeks before stopping exactly at $22 a barrel, a critical support level and a four-month low.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil producer, is standing by its bullish outlook for oil prices this year, according to Gulf sources.
The sources, familiar with oil policy in the kingdom and other key Middle East producers Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, said Brent should "easily" average between $20 and $25 a barrel in 1997.
They said the Saudis and other Gulf Arab producers were content to allow oil prices to drift to the top of that range without considering raising their output.

"The need to build gasoline stocks coincides with heavy refinery maintenance work in the U.S. Then by the third quarter, the market will again focus on heating oil. It all looks positive for the price," a Saudi source said.
